sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The reflection machinery: encoding/json uses reflection over the struct's fields at runtime — reading the tags, matching JSON keys to Go fields (case-insensitive fallback), building the encoder/decoder per type. The cost: reflection is ~10-100x slower than a hand-written converter — the price of the universal 'any struct, any JSON, zero codegen.' For hot paths, the alternatives (easyjson codegen, json-iterator) exist; for 95% of services, the reflection cost is noise.

The field-matching subtleties: unmarshal matches JSON keys to Go fields case-insensitively when there's no exact tag match — {"Name":...} fills the Name field even with the json:"name" tag (the tag's key match is exact; the fallback is case-insensitive). Unexported fields are never serialized (the `notes string` field in our demo — invisible to JSON). Unmatched JSON keys are silently dropped — strictness requires DisallowUnknownFields (the Decoder option) when the contract needs enforcing.

The omitempty's semantics, precisely: it omits when the value is the TYPE'S ZERO — 0, "", nil, false, empty slice/map, nil pointer. It cannot express 'omit when the value is semantically empty-but-nonzero' (0 is a valid age; omitempty hides it). For that: pointer fields (*int — nil is omitted, *int(0) is included) or custom marshaling (MarshalJSON on the type). The pointer trick is the standard answer for '0 is a legitimate value.'
